text: Espoo. A recruitment evening. Four companies, ten talents, fifteen minutes per conversation.
This is Fatima. She was a pharmacy assistant, then she learned to code in a bootcamp.
And this is Kaarna Health, a small Espoo start-up looking for a junior web developer.
Fatima's CV was polished by AI, like everyone else's. Kaarna can't tell what is real.
Rosace puts job requirements and declared skills on the same map: Kaarna sets the level each skill needs, and Fatima shows the level she declares.
Rosace matches the two, then checks each skill: before the meeting with a short exercise, or during the conversation with a targeted question. The recruiter decides.
Rosace has three spaces: the company describes its need, the talent builds a skills card, and the organiser prepares the meetings.
Everyone uses the same twelve skills, in five families. That is the rosace.
Each level describes a real situation. Get it right, Intermediate: your work passes review with few corrections.
The company picks its three most important skills, in gold.
Fatima's declared level is drawn dotted. What a recruiter actually observes is drawn solid, branch by branch.
Kaarna drops in its job post. Claude proposes the key skills and quotes the job text. The recruiter accepts.
The recruiter stays in charge: for a junior, Kaarna makes Keep commitments a major.
Each skill already says how it will be checked: an online exercise before the event, or a question at the meeting.
Fatima imports her CV. It never leaves her device. Rosace points to clues, and she declares each level herself.
There is no ranking. For each company, people are suggested or need more information, always with the reasons. Fatima is suggested for Kaarna, and the organiser approves the meeting.
At the meeting, the recruiter has questions and short situations to check the other skills.
Afterwards, the recruiter notes what was seen, skill by skill. Observed stays separate from what Fatima declared.
Rosace only suggests, and always shows why. A person decides.

Rosace has tests built in. Before the event, the recruiter picks short online exercises, twenty minutes at most. Fatima answers one. Claude suggests a grade with evidence, and the recruiter gives the final grade.
Before the event, Fatima takes a short timed exercise, at the level she declared. She spots the boundary bug, fixes the condition and proposes tests.
Claude reviews her answer against clear criteria and suggests a grade with evidence. Here: C, seen in part. The recruiter reads it and confirms.
Only this skill changes. A means seen clearly, C seen in part, F not seen, NE not covered.
A clearer reason to meet. Concrete skills to discuss. A human decision.
